title: Networking Essentials
subtitle: 40 questions covering all key topics. Shuffled each attempt.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of the OSI model in networking?
opts: To define hardware specifications for network cables
To provide layered abstractions for reasoning about device communication
questions.expl: The OSI model is a layered architecture that lets application developers reason about network communication in simpler, abstracted terms without needing to understand lower-level details like electrical signals.

questions.q: Which OSI layer is IP (Internet Protocol) primarily associated with?
questions.expl: IP operates at Layer 3 (Network layer). It handles routing and addressing, breaks data into packets, and provides best-effort delivery to any destination IP address.

questions.q: Which of the following protocols operates at the Application Layer (Layer 7)?
questions.expl: HTTP, DNS, WebSockets, and WebRTC are all application-layer protocols (Layer 7). TCP and UDP are transport-layer (Layer 4) and IP is network-layer (Layer 3).

questions.q: What is the first step in a simple web request when you type a URL into a browser?
questions.expl: DNS Resolution happens first — the browser converts the human-readable domain name (e.g. hellointerview.com) into an IP address before any TCP connection can be established.

questions.q: How many steps are in the TCP three-way handshake?
questions.expl: The TCP three-way handshake consists of SYN (client to server), SYN-ACK (server to client), and ACK (client to server). This establishes the connection before data transfer begins.

questions.q: What does 'stateless' mean in the context of HTTP?
opts: Each request is independent; the server doesn't maintain info about prior requests
The server maintains a record of all requests
questions.expl: HTTP is stateless — each request stands on its own and the server doesn't need to remember any previous interactions. This simplifies server design and is generally desirable in system design.

questions.q: What is the TCP teardown sequence after data transfer completes?
questions.expl: TCP uses a four-way teardown: FIN (client), ACK (server), FIN (server), ACK (client). Both sides must explicitly close their end of the connection.

questions.q: Which protocol is described as 'connectionless' with no guarantees of delivery or ordering?
questions.expl: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and provides no guarantees for delivery, ordering, or duplicate protection. It's fast but 'spray and pray' in nature.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of TCP?
questions.expl: TCP guarantees ordered delivery — messages sent in the same connection arrive in the same order. 'No ordering guarantees' is a characteristic of UDP, not TCP.

questions.q: What is the header size of a UDP packet?
questions.expl: UDP has a very small 8-byte header, contributing to its lower overhead and faster transmission compared to TCP's 20–60 byte header.

questions.q: Which protocol would be the best fit for a live video streaming application where some packet loss is acceptable?
questions.expl: UDP is ideal for live video streaming because speed and low latency matter more than perfect reliability. The client can handle occasional dropped packets (e.g. a brief visual glitch) rather than waiting for retransmission.

questions.q: QUIC is best described as which of the following?
opts: An older replacement for UDP with no handshake
A new protocol combining some TCP reliability benefits with modernization and performance improvements
questions.expl: QUIC is a relatively new transport protocol that aims to provide similar reliability benefits to TCP while adding performance improvements. It's becoming more popular but not yet ubiquitous.

questions.q: In which scenario would you likely choose TCP over UDP?
questions.expl: TCP is ideal when data integrity is critical. A payment API must guarantee every byte is delivered correctly and in order — packet loss would be catastrophic. Gaming, VoIP, and DNS can tolerate some loss.

questions.q: What does 'congestion control' in TCP refer to?
opts: Preventing clients from sending too many DNS requests
Adapting data transmission rate to avoid overwhelming the network during congestion
Limiting the number of HTTP connections per user
questions.expl: TCP's congestion control mechanism monitors network conditions and reduces transmission rate when congestion is detected, helping prevent network collapse from overload.

questions.q: Which HTTP method should be idempotent and have no request body?
questions.expl: GET requests should be idempotent (calling them multiple times has no side effects) and don't have a request body. They are used to retrieve data from a server.

questions.q: What HTTP status code indicates a resource was successfully created?
questions.expl: 201 Created is returned when a POST request successfully creates a new resource. 200 OK is for general success, not specifically resource creation.

questions.q: Which status code means the client has sent too many requests in a given period?
questions.expl: 429 Too Many Requests is the standard rate-limiting status code, indicating the client has exceeded the allowed number of requests in a time window.

questions.q: In REST API design, how would you correctly represent 'get all posts for a user'?
questions.expl: RESTful APIs model resources and relationships. GET /users/{id}/posts uses proper HTTP verb + nested resource path to represent fetching posts belonging to a specific user.

questions.q: What does HTTPS add over HTTP?
opts: A TLS/SSL security layer that encrypts communications
questions.expl: HTTPS adds TLS/SSL encryption on top of HTTP, protecting data in transit against eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks. All public-facing websites should use HTTPS.

questions.q: What is the main design principle of REST APIs?
opts: All endpoints use POST with JSON bodies
Clients perform simple CRUD operations on resources using HTTP verbs
Every API must be versioned with /v1/ prefix
questions.expl: REST is built around the idea that clients perform simple operations (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on resources, using HTTP methods as verbs and URL paths to identify those resources.

questions.q: What is a key security risk to watch for even with HTTPS?
opts: Request bodies are encrypted but the server should still validate user IDs and not trust them blindly
HTTPS slows down all APIs significantly
HTTP status codes are visible to attackers
questions.expl: HTTPS encrypts data in transit but doesn't guarantee that request contents were generated by a legitimate client. Servers must always validate input — an attacker could modify the request body to change a user ID and access arbitrary data.

questions.q: What problem does GraphQL primarily solve?
opts: Over-fetching and under-fetching of data in APIs
questions.expl: GraphQL solves the over-fetching (getting more data than needed) and under-fetching (needing multiple requests to get all required data) problems common with REST APIs by letting clients request exactly the data they need.

questions.q: What serialization format does gRPC use instead of JSON?
questions.expl: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers — a binary encoding that is more compact (fewer bytes) and faster to parse than JSON. Benchmarks show gRPC can achieve up to 10x throughput over JSON/HTTP.

questions.q: Which transport protocol does gRPC build upon?
questions.expl: gRPC uses HTTP/2 as its transport protocol, which enables features like multiplexing, streaming, and header compression that contribute to its high performance.

questions.q: When is gRPC most appropriate according to the article?
opts: Internal service-to-service communication where performance is critical
questions.expl: gRPC shines for internal microservice communication where efficiency and strong typing matter. It's generally not used for public-facing APIs because it's a binary protocol with less accessible tooling for external clients.

questions.q: What is the recommended default API choice for system design interviews?
questions.expl: REST is the recommended default for system design interviews. It's well-understood, flexible, and a good baseline. You should only reach for GraphQL, gRPC, SSE, or WebSockets when REST can't meet specific requirements.

questions.q: How does Server-Sent Events (SSE) work at the transport level?
opts: It uses a persistent UDP connection for fast pushing
It opens a new HTTP connection for every event
It streams many messages as 'chunks' over a single HTTP response connection
It requires a WebSocket upgrade handshake
questions.expl: SSE is a hack on top of HTTP — the server keeps a single HTTP response open and streams messages as individual lines (chunks) over time. The client processes each line as it arrives.

questions.q: Which of the following is a known limitation of SSE?
opts: It requires a special UDP socket
Servers or load balancers may close long-lived connections; the EventSource reconnects automatically
It only works with gRPC backends
It cannot be used over HTTPS
questions.expl: SSE connections can be closed by servers, load balancers, or proxy middleboxes. The SSE standard handles this with an EventSource object that automatically reconnects with the last received message ID.

questions.q: What makes WebSockets different from SSE?
opts: WebSockets use UDP instead of TCP
WebSockets support bidirectional communication; SSE is server-to-client only
WebSockets are faster because they avoid HTTP entirely
SSE supports binary data but WebSockets do not
questions.expl: WebSockets provide persistent, bidirectional (full-duplex) communication — both client and server can send messages freely. SSE is unidirectional: only the server can push data to the client.

questions.q: How is a WebSocket connection initiated?
opts: By sending a UDP packet to the server
Via a TCP SYN to a dedicated WebSocket port
Via an HTTP 'upgrade' protocol that upgrades an existing TCP connection
Via DNS lookup to find the WebSocket endpoint
questions.expl: WebSockets start as a regular HTTP connection which then performs an 'upgrade' handshake to switch to the WebSocket protocol over the same TCP connection. This allows reusing HTTP session info like cookies.

questions.q: Which protocol is best suited for audio/video calling applications?
questions.expl: WebRTC is specifically designed for peer-to-peer audio/video communication between browsers. It uses UDP for low-latency media transfer and includes built-in mechanisms for NAT traversal.

questions.q: What does STUN stand for in the context of WebRTC?
questions.expl: STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT) is a protocol used in WebRTC to help peers discover their public IP addresses and ports, enabling direct peer-to-peer connections even when behind NAT devices.

questions.q: What is the role of a signaling server in WebRTC?
opts: It relays all audio/video data between peers
It keeps track of available peers and their connection information so they can find each other
It assigns IP addresses via DHCP
questions.expl: The WebRTC signaling server is a central coordination point where peers register and exchange connection information. Once peers find each other, the actual media flows directly peer-to-peer (bypassing the signaling server).

questions.q: What is 'client-side load balancing'?
opts: The client browser randomly picks a CSS file to load
The client itself decides which backend server to contact, often using a service registry
A load balancer sitting in front of all clients
DNS always pointing to one fixed server
questions.expl: With client-side load balancing, clients query a service registry for a list of available servers and then make routing decisions themselves — without an intermediary. This avoids an extra network hop per request.

questions.q: At which OSI layer do Layer 4 load balancers operate?
questions.expl: Layer 4 load balancers operate at the Transport layer (TCP/UDP). They route based on IP addresses and ports without inspecting the actual content of packets.

questions.q: What is a key advantage of L7 load balancers over L4 load balancers?
opts: They are faster due to zero packet inspection
They maintain persistent TCP connections more efficiently
They can route based on HTTP request content like URLs, headers, and cookies
They use less CPU than L4 balancers
questions.expl: L7 load balancers understand the application layer (HTTP) and can make intelligent routing decisions based on request content — e.g. routing /api requests to one server farm and static assets to another.

questions.q: Which load balancing algorithm is recommended for services with persistent connections like WebSockets?
questions.expl: Least Connections is preferred for persistent-connection services (SSE, WebSockets) because it prevents a single server from gradually accumulating all long-lived connections while others stay idle.

questions.q: How does DNS contribute to load balancing?
opts: DNS servers run load balancer software on their own
DNS returns a rotated list of IP addresses so different clients hit different servers
DNS caches all responses forever, eliminating load
DNS only works with a single IP per domain
questions.expl: DNS-based load balancing works by returning different IP addresses (or different orderings) to different clients. Each client gets a rotated list, naturally distributing traffic across multiple servers.

questions.q: What is the purpose of health checks in a load balancer?
opts: To measure the latency of DNS resolution
To determine if backend servers are healthy and route traffic away from failed ones
To encrypt HTTP traffic between client and server
To limit the number of connections per client
questions.expl: Health checks allow load balancers to detect failed or unhealthy servers and automatically stop routing traffic to them until they recover. This enables automatic failover without manual intervention.

questions.q: What is 'exponential backoff' in retry strategies?
opts: Retrying at a fixed interval forever until success
Doubling the wait time between each retry attempt to reduce load on recovering services
Immediately retrying failed requests with no delay
Canceling all retries after the first failure
questions.expl: Exponential backoff increases the wait time between retries (e.g. 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...), giving struggling services time to recover and reducing the retry storm that could make things worse.

questions.q: Why is 'jitter' important in retry strategies?
opts: It adds randomness to retry timing to prevent all clients from retrying simultaneously
It speeds up the initial connection
questions.expl: Jitter adds randomness to backoff timings so that multiple clients don't synchronize their retries and hammer a recovering service all at once — a 'thundering herd' that could prevent recovery.

questions.q: What is an idempotency key used for?
opts: Ensuring an operation is only processed once even if the request is retried multiple times
Tracking the number of API calls per user
questions.expl: An idempotency key is a unique identifier sent with a request that lets the server detect and deduplicate retried requests — preventing side effects like double-charging a user's credit card.

questions.q: In a circuit breaker pattern, what does the 'open' state mean?
opts: Requests flow normally to the downstream service
The circuit has tripped and requests immediately fail without attempting the actual call
The service is under test with partial traffic
The load balancer is sending extra health checks
questions.expl: When a circuit breaker trips to 'open' state (because failures exceeded a threshold), requests immediately fail-fast without even attempting the network call. This prevents cascading failures and reduces load on the struggling service.

questions.q: What is the 'half-open' state in a circuit breaker?
opts: Half of all requests are blocked
The circuit breaker sends a single test request to check if the service has recovered
Retries happen at half the normal rate
The load balancer routes 50% of traffic to the failed service
questions.expl: After an open circuit's timeout period, it transitions to 'half-open' and sends a single test request. If it succeeds, the circuit closes (normal operation resumes); if it fails, the circuit reopens.

questions.q: What is the theoretical minimum round-trip latency between New York and London due to physics?
questions.expl: Light travels through fiber at ~2/3 the speed of light in vacuum (~200,000 km/s). The ~5,600 km New York–London distance gives a theoretical minimum of ~56ms round-trip — before any processing time is added.

questions.q: What is a CDN 'edge location'?
opts: A server at the CDN's headquarters
A geographically distributed server close to end users that caches content
A firewall appliance at a data center
A load balancer for DNS requests
questions.expl: Edge locations are CDN servers distributed around the world, positioned close to users. When a user's request can be served from a nearby edge server (via caching), they get very low latency responses.

questions.q: What strategy does Uber's system design use to minimize cross-region data queries?
opts: Replicating all data to every data center worldwide
Regional partitioning — grouping nearby cities and co-locating their data and servers
Using UDP for all location updates
questions.expl: Regional partitioning co-locates data and servers for nearby geographic areas. Since an Uber rider in Miami will never book a driver in New York, queries can be answered entirely within a regional cluster — fast and efficient.
